name: WLKATA Mirobot Education Kit
description: A compact 6-axis desktop robot arm styled after full-size industrial arms like the ABB IRB 6700, built around stepper-motor joints and an Arduino-based controller. Sold in an "Education Kit" configuration bundling a pen holder, pneumatic and servo grippers, and in-house STEM curriculum materials. Originally crowdfunded on Kickstarter as an "open-source" arm in 2019, though the actual arm firmware is now proprietary — only its PC-side Python SDK carries a genuine open-source license.

specs.label: Software
specs.note: current SDK is genuinely MIT-licensed; the arm's own firmware is proprietary

specs.label: Degrees of Freedom
specs.note: 6 rotational joints + a separate gripper open/close axis — a true 6-axis arm

specs.note: open-loop steppers on all 6 joints — no motor brand/model disclosed

sourcing: Specs compiled from WLKATA's official product and spec pages, RobotShop, Oz Robotics, and Geyer Instructional listings, WLKATA's GitHub organization (LICENSE files verified directly for both the Python SDK and the Firmware repo), and independent commentary (the0x00.dev, RenderHub). Several details are flagged as unconfirmed above: WLKATA's own founder/corporate-structure claims, the exact meaning of the base-joint "M6" sticker, whether the base Mirobot (as opposed to its MiroMAX successor) actually speaks Modbus over its RS485 connection, and current live Amazon pricing. The Open Source badge here covers WLKATA's current Python SDK only, not the arm's proprietary firmware.

pricing.summary: WLKATA's own store lists the Education Kit configuration pictured here at **$1,680**, matched by RobotShop and Geyer Instructional (Oz Robotics discounts it to roughly **$1,613**), with a Professional Kit tier adding a wireless Bluetooth teach pendant for **$1,776–$1,850**. Add-on modules are sold separately and can add thousands more, from an AI Vision Set ($890) up to an OpenCV Advanced Vision Suite ($4,990), so the base price alone understates full cost for many use cases.

editorial.heading: Insights
editorial.body: Despite being marketed and sold as "open source" — including in current reseller listings — WLKATA's own firmware repository states outright, "Proprietary firmware. All rights reserved by WLKATA"; only the separate PC-side Python SDK genuinely carries an MIT license, not the arm's firmware or hardware design.

firmwareCommunity.note: WLKATA's own genuinely open-source, PC-side Python SDK for controlling Mirobot; the arm's onboard firmware itself is proprietary.
